Likely Causes: Infection (viral/bacterial), inflammation, heat exhaustion, immune response
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Temp above 103°F/39.4°C, stiff neck, confusion, difficulty breathing, seizure
Self-Care Tips: Rest, fluids, light clothing, paracetamol/acetaminophen per label
Male-Specific Notes: May spike higher; higher metabolic rate. Recovery typically 5-7 days
Female-Specific Notes: Hormonal cycle affects baseline temp. Higher in luteal phase. May worsen PMS
When to See a Doctor: Fever lasts >3 days, or in infants under 3 months with any fever

Likely Causes: Poor sleep, anemia, stress, thyroid issues, viral illness, overtraining

Self-Care Tips: Prioritize sleep, hydrate, balanced meals, moderate activity
Male-Specific Notes: Often indicates infection or serious condition. May mask depression initially
Female-Specific Notes: Common with anemia, thyroid issues, hormonal imbalances, menstrual cycle. Iron deficiency more common
When to See a Doctor: Persists beyond 2 weeks or interferes with daily life

Likely Causes: Fever onset, cold exposure, infection
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Chills with high fever and confusion
Self-Care Tips: Warm layers, warm fluids, rest
When to See a Doctor: Recurrent chills with fever over 48 hours

Likely Causes: Infection, hormonal changes, medication side effect, anxiety
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Drenching sweats with unexplained weight loss or fever
Self-Care Tips: Breathable bedding/clothing, track frequency
When to See a Doctor: Occurs regularly for more than a week

Likely Causes: Metabolic changes, chronic illness, stress, thyroid issues
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Weight loss with persistent pain, blood in stool, or severe fatigue
Self-Care Tips: Track diet and weight; ensure adequate calorie intake
When to See a Doctor: Loss of more than 5% body weight in 6-12 months

Likely Causes: Illness, stress, medication, digestive upset
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Combined with severe abdominal pain or vomiting
Self-Care Tips: Small frequent meals, stay hydrated
When to See a Doctor: Lasts more than a week or causes noticeable weight loss

Likely Causes: Tension, dehydration, eye strain, migraine, sinus congestion
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Sudden 'worst-ever' headache, headache with fever/stiff neck, or after head injury
Self-Care Tips: Rest in dark quiet room, hydration, OTC pain relief
Male-Specific Notes: Often tension-type. Less likely migraine (except cluster headaches more common)
Female-Specific Notes: Migraines 3x more common. Hormonal fluctuations trigger migraines. Estrogen withdrawal effect
When to See a Doctor: Frequent, worsening, or unlike usual headaches

Likely Causes: Dehydration, low blood pressure, inner ear issues, low blood sugar
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Dizziness with chest pain, slurred speech, or one-sided weakness
Self-Care Tips: Sit/lie down, hydrate, avoid sudden movements
When to See a Doctor: Recurrent episodes or accompanied by fainting

Likely Causes: Triggers: stress, hormones, certain foods, sleep changes
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Sudden severe migraine unlike prior ones, with confusion or vision loss
Self-Care Tips: Dark quiet rest, hydration, known trigger avoidance
When to See a Doctor: Migraines increasing in frequency or severity

Likely Causes: Nerve compression, poor circulation, vitamin deficiency
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Sudden numbness on one side of body, face drooping, slurred speech
Self-Care Tips: Change position, gentle stretching
When to See a Doctor: Persistent, spreading, or affecting one side suddenly

Likely Causes: Epilepsy, high fever (children), head injury, low blood sugar
Commonly Co-occurs With: Confusion, loss of consciousness, muscle jerking
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Any first-time seizure, seizure lasting over 5 minutes, or repeated seizures
Self-Care Tips: Move away from hazards, do not restrain, time the episode
When to See a Doctor: Always requires medical evaluation

Likely Causes: Fatigue, dehydration, stress, medication side effects, aging
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Sudden confusion, especially with fever, head injury, or slurred speech
Self-Care Tips: Rest, hydration, reduce distractions
When to See a Doctor: Sudden onset or progressively worsening confusion

Likely Causes: Viral infection, allergies, irritants, acid reflux
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Cough with blood, severe breathlessness, or chest pain

When to See a Doctor: Lasts more than 3 weeks

Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Green/bloody phlegm with high fever and breathlessness
Self-Care Tips: Fluids, rest, steam inhalation
When to See a Doctor: Phlegm is discolored/bloody or persists beyond 10 days

Likely Causes: Asthma, anxiety, chest infection, exertion, heart issues
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Sudden severe breathlessness, blue lips, chest pain
Self-Care Tips: Sit upright, slow breathing, use prescribed inhaler if applicable
Male-Specific Notes: Usually indicates cardiac/pulmonary pathology. Take seriously
Female-Specific Notes: May be anxiety-related. Pregnancy-related dyspnea normal. Iron deficiency anemia contribution
When to See a Doctor: Any unexplained or worsening breathlessness

Likely Causes: Asthma, allergies, respiratory infection
Commonly Co-occurs With: Cough, chest tightness, shortness of breath
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Wheezing with severe breathing difficulty or blue lips
Self-Care Tips: Avoid triggers, use prescribed inhaler if applicable
When to See a Doctor: New or worsening wheeze, especially in children

Likely Causes: Viral infection, strep throat, allergies, dry air
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Difficulty swallowing/breathing, drooling, high fever
Self-Care Tips: Warm salt water gargle, fluids, throat lozenges
Male-Specific Notes: Similar presentation. Slightly higher risk of strep in children
Female-Specific Notes: May worsen with hormonal cycle. Consider candida with certain contraceptives
When to See a Doctor: Lasts more than a week or very severe pain

Likely Causes: Common cold, allergies, sinus infection
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Thick discolored discharge with facial pain and fever
Self-Care Tips: Saline rinse, fluids, rest
When to See a Doctor: Persists beyond 10 days or with facial pain

Likely Causes: Ear infection, fluid buildup, wax blockage, air pressure changes
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Severe pain with high fever, swelling behind ear, or fluid discharge

When to See a Doctor: Pain persists over 2 days or with fever/discharge

Likely Causes: Wax buildup, infection, loud noise exposure, aging
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Sudden hearing loss in one or both ears
Self-Care Tips: Avoid loud noise, do not use cotton swabs deep in ear
When to See a Doctor: Sudden or unexplained hearing loss

Likely Causes: Viral infection, sinus congestion, nasal polyps
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Sudden loss with no other symptoms lasting weeks
Self-Care Tips: Saline rinse, allow infection to resolve
When to See a Doctor: Persists beyond 2 weeks

Likely Causes: Muscle strain, acid reflux, anxiety, heart-related causes
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Pressure/tightness radiating to arm/jaw, sweating, breathlessness
Self-Care Tips: Rest and stop exertion; do not self-diagnose
Male-Specific Notes: Classic crushing/pressure pain more likely. Higher cardiac risk age 45+
Female-Specific Notes: Often atypical: sharp, indigestion-like, fatigue, shortness of breath. Higher risk postmenopause
When to See a Doctor: Any unexplained chest pain warrants prompt evaluation

Likely Causes: Caffeine, stress, dehydration, anxiety, heart rhythm issues
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Palpitations with fainting, chest pain, or breathlessness
Self-Care Tips: Reduce caffeine/stimulants, relax, hydrate
When to See a Doctor: Frequent, prolonged, or with fainting/chest pain

Likely Causes: Prolonged standing/sitting, poor circulation, heart/kidney issues
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Sudden one-leg swelling with pain/warmth (possible clot), or breathlessness
Self-Care Tips: Elevate legs, reduce salt intake, move regularly
When to See a Doctor: Sudden, one-sided, or with breathing difficulty

Likely Causes: Diet, stress, genetics, lack of activity
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Severe headache with vision changes, chest pain, or confusion
Self-Care Tips: Reduce salt/stress, regular monitoring, activity
When to See a Doctor: Readings consistently above normal range

Likely Causes: Motion sickness, infection, food intolerance, pregnancy, anxiety

Self-Care Tips: Small sips of fluids, ginger, bland food
Male-Specific Notes: Primarily GI or medication-related. Less common overall
Female-Specific Notes: Consider pregnancy, hormonal contraceptives, hormonal cycle. Morning sickness in pregnancy

Likely Causes: Infection, food poisoning, motion sickness, migraine
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Blood in vomit, signs of dehydration, severe abdominal pain
Self-Care Tips: Sip clear fluids, rest stomach, bland diet when able
When to See a Doctor: Lasts more than 24 hours or with dehydration signs

Likely Causes: Infection, food intolerance, medication side effect, stress
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Blood in stool, high fever, signs of severe dehydration
Self-Care Tips: Oral rehydration fluids, bland diet (BRAT), rest
When to See a Doctor: Lasts more than 2 days or with blood/fever

Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Severe pain, inability to pass gas/stool, vomiting
Self-Care Tips: Increase fiber and water intake, gentle activity
When to See a Doctor: Lasts more than a week or with severe pain

Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Severe/localized pain (esp. lower right), rigid abdomen, fever
Self-Care Tips: Rest, light diet, warm compress
Male-Specific Notes: Consider appendicitis, kidney stones, IBS equally
Female-Specific Notes: Consider menstrual cramping, ovulation pain, endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease
When to See a Doctor: Severe, persistent, or localized pain

Likely Causes: Diet, food intolerance, swallowing air, digestive disorders
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Bloating with severe pain or vomiting
Self-Care Tips: Smaller meals, limit gas-producing foods, gentle walking
When to See a Doctor: Persistent or worsening despite diet changes

Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Chest pain that could mimic heart issues, difficulty swallowing
Self-Care Tips: Smaller meals, avoid trigger foods, don't lie down right after eating
When to See a Doctor: Frequent (2+ times/week) or worsening

Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Large amounts of blood, black tarry stool, dizziness/fainting
Self-Care Tips: Note color/amount, avoid straining
When to See a Doctor: Any occurrence should be medically evaluated

Likely Causes: Overuse, arthritis, injury, inflammation
Commonly Co-occurs With: Swelling, stiffness, reduced range of motion

Self-Care Tips: Rest, ice/heat, gentle movement, OTC pain relief

Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Severe pain with swelling, weakness, or dark urine

When to See a Doctor: Persists beyond a week or is severe

Self-Care Tips: Rest briefly then gentle movement, heat/ice, posture correction

Female-Specific Notes: Pregnancy-related sacroiliac pain common. Osteoporosis risk postmenopause

Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Stiff neck with high fever and headache (possible meningitis)
Self-Care Tips: Gentle stretching, warm compress, posture adjustment
When to See a Doctor: With fever/headache, or lasts beyond a week

Likely Causes: Injury, arthritis, infection, overuse

When to See a Doctor: Persistent swelling or with fever

Likely Causes: Overuse, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, nerve issues
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Sudden one-sided weakness, facial drooping, slurred speech
Self-Care Tips: Rest, hydrate, balanced electrolytes
When to See a Doctor: Sudden onset or progressively worsening

Male-Specific Notes: Often fungal (jock itch) or contact dermatitis
Female-Specific Notes: Yeast infections more common. Hormonal triggers. Cosmetics/product reactions
When to See a Doctor: Spreads, blisters, or doesn't improve in a few days

Likely Causes: Dry skin, allergic reaction, insect bite, irritant
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Itching with widespread hives and breathing difficulty
Self-Care Tips: Moisturize, avoid scratching, cool compress
When to See a Doctor: Persistent, widespread, or affecting sleep

Likely Causes: Allergic reaction, stress, infection, food/medication trigger
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Hives with facial/throat swelling or breathing difficulty (anaphylaxis)
Self-Care Tips: Antihistamine per label, avoid trigger, cool compress
When to See a Doctor: Widespread, recurring, or with swelling of face/throat

Likely Causes: Weather, dehydration, harsh soap, skin conditions
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Cracking with signs of infection (redness, pus)
Self-Care Tips: Moisturize regularly, lukewarm showers, hydrate
When to See a Doctor: Persistent cracking or signs of infection

Likely Causes: Minor trauma, blood thinners, vitamin deficiency, clotting issues
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Bruising with no clear cause, or with unusual bleeding elsewhere
Self-Care Tips: Ice pack initially, elevate area, monitor
When to See a Doctor: Frequent unexplained bruising

Likely Causes: Urinary tract infection, irritation, dehydration
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Pain with fever, back pain, or blood in urine
Self-Care Tips: Increase water intake, avoid irritants (caffeine/alcohol)
When to See a Doctor: Persists beyond a day or with fever

Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Frequent urination with excessive thirst and fatigue (possible diabetes signs)
Self-Care Tips: Monitor fluid intake, avoid bladder irritants
When to See a Doctor: Sudden change in pattern or with other symptoms

Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Blood in urine with severe pain or inability to urinate
Self-Care Tips: Note frequency/amount, stay hydrated
When to See a Doctor: Any occurrence should be medically evaluated

Likely Causes: Stress, hormonal changes, weight changes, underlying conditions
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Severe pain, very heavy bleeding, or bleeding after menopause
Self-Care Tips: Track cycle, manage stress, balanced diet
When to See a Doctor: Persistent irregularity or very heavy/painful periods

Self-Care Tips: Breathing exercises, reduce stimulants, talk to someone trusted
Male-Specific Notes: Often presents as irritability/anger. Underdiagnosed. May manifest as physical symptoms
Female-Specific Notes: More likely diagnosed. Linked to hormonal cycles. Postpartum anxiety/depression common

When to See a Doctor: Persists beyond 3-4 weeks

Likely Causes: Stress, life events, underlying mood disorder
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Thoughts of self-harm or hopelessness
Self-Care Tips: Stay connected with others, gentle routine, sunlight/activity
When to See a Doctor: Persists beyond 2 weeks or affects daily functioning

Likely Causes: Eye strain, dry eyes, refractive error, migraine
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Sudden vision loss/change, especially one-sided

When to See a Doctor: Sudden onset or persistent change

Likely Causes: Allergies, dryness, infection (conjunctivitis), irritant exposure
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Severe pain, vision changes, or thick discharge
Self-Care Tips: Cool compress, avoid rubbing, artificial tears
When to See a Doctor: Persists beyond a few days or with pain/vision changes

Red Flag / Emergency Signs: With severe eye pain or sudden vision change
Self-Care Tips: Dim lighting, sunglasses outdoors, rest eyes
When to See a Doctor: Persistent or with headache/vision changes

Female-Specific Notes: May worsen with hormonal cycle. Consider candida with certain contraceptives

Female-Specific Notes: Hormonal nasal congestion during menstrual cycle. Pregnancy rhinitis common

Male-Specific Notes: Primarily GI or medication-related. Less common overall
Female-Specific Notes: Consider pregnancy, hormonal contraceptives, hormonal cycle. Morning sickness in pregnancy

Female-Specific Notes: Often atypical: sharp, indigestion-like, fatigue, shortness of breath. Higher risk postmenopause

Female-Specific Notes: May be anxiety-related. Pregnancy-related dyspnea normal. Iron deficiency anemia contribution

Female-Specific Notes: Consider menstrual cramping, ovulation pain, endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease

Female-Specific Notes: Pregnancy-related sacroiliac pain common. Osteoporosis risk postmenopause
